claim: Apple and Google are jointly building a DMA-mandated cross-OS 'device transfer' solution to move contacts, calendar, messages, photos, documents, Wi-Fi networks, passwords, and third-party app data between iPhone and Android, explicitly to 'reduce data lock-in and unlock user choice' — this targets the specific form of switching cost (abandoning purchased apps/data/photos) that the thesis identifies as the load-bearing lock-in mechanism, distinct from browser switching.
stance_target: ecosystem lock-in via data/app abandonment costs is structural and immune to regulatory intervention
scope_conditions: Worldwide rollout (per Commission factsheet), as of May 2026, tool still in developer beta
quoted_support: Taken together, the device and eSIM transfer solutions will reduce data lock-in and unlock user choice. Users will be able to choose a new phone based on the innovative features they value, without being locked into an ecosystem due to the complexities associated with transferring their data.

claim: As of the May 2026 Commission factsheet, the cross-OS device transfer tool (AppMigrationKit) is still in beta/documentation stage for developers with no reported usage or adoption statistics — the capability to reduce phone-switching costs exists, but no measured behavioral switching response has yet been published.
stance_target: whether phone-switching costs have actually fallen in practice, versus merely having the legal/technical capability to fall
quoted_support: Apple overviewed this project in its DMA compliance reports and has now made the relevant documentation available to developers in beta (AppMigrationKit).

claim: Apple and Google rolled out a live eSIM and phone-number transfer solution in 2025, already supported by several European and non-European carriers, simplifying carrier continuity when switching between iPhone and Android — a concrete, already-live (not merely proposed) reduction in one component of phone-switching friction.
stance_target: phone-switching costs remain entirely structural and unaddressed by regulation
quoted_support: This solution will follow Apple's and Google's rollout of the eSIM transfer solution in 2025, which greatly simplified the transfer of eSIMs and phone numbers between iPhones and Android phones (and vice versa).

claim: The DMA's Article 6(7) interoperability requirement is forcing Apple to open iOS features previously exclusive to Apple-branded connected devices (Apple Watch, AirPods) to third-party accessory makers — including notifications, proximity pairing, and automatic audio switching, with binding Commission deadlines (1 June 2026 and 1 June 2027) following a 19 March 2025 Commission decision on connected devices.
stance_target: Apple's hardware-ecosystem integration advantage is immune to regulatory unwinding
scope_conditions: EU iOS connected-device ecosystem, Commission decision 19 March 2025, deadlines June 2026-2027
quoted_support: Following the Commission's decision on connected devices of 19 March 2025, Apple must release interoperability solutions for some key iOS features to allow developers and connected device providers to offer European users the same experience as with Apple's devices.
numbers: 1 June 2027 deadline for audio switching expansion

claim: No EU-vs-non-EU or before/after empirical data exists (in this document or elsewhere found in this research batch) measuring actual iOS-to-Android switching RATES — only the removal of switching-cost infrastructure barriers is documented, not the resulting behavioral response. This is a genuine evidentiary absence relevant to testing whether the DMA natural experiment addresses phone-level (not just browser-level) lock-in.
stance_target: the natural experiment tests a weaker form of lock-in (browser) than the thesis needs (phone/device ecosystem)
scope_conditions: Searched EC official documentation and web sources as of September 2026; no switching-rate study located
quoted_support: [ABSENCE FINDING — no verbatim quote available; this is a recorded gap in coverage after searching EC factsheets, press materials, and general web search for 'iOS to Android switching rate EU DMA versus non-EU markets']
